references.text: The Pharisees and the scribes also grumbled previously that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, using exactly the same accusatory question: "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?" ([ref:Luk 5:30|Luke 5:30]).

When Jesus went to Zacchaeus's home, people grumbled and said: "He has gone in to stay with a sinful man." The same pattern of criticism against Jesus having fellowship with sinners ([ref:Luk 19:7|Luke 19:7]).
Jesus himself described how he was criticized as "a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners" ([ref:Luk 7:34|Luke 7:34]).
The Pharisees asked the disciples: "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" – a parallel to the criticism in Luke 15:2 ([ref:Matt 9:11|Matthew 9:11]).
The scribes among the Pharisees criticized Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners – a direct parallel to the accusation in Luke 15:2 ([ref:Mark 2:16|Mark 2:16]).
The context of the grumbling: tax collectors and sinners stayed close to Jesus to hear him, which triggered the reaction of the Pharisees and the scribes ([ref:Luk 15:1|Luke 15:1]).
The Pharisee Simon thought that Jesus should have known that the woman who touched him was a sinner – the same attitude that Jesus should not have contact with sinners ([ref:Luk 7:39|Luke 7:39]).

Paul reflects on the distinction between Jews and "sinners from the Gentiles", which mirrors the Pharisees' tendency to set up sharp boundaries against those they regarded as sinners ([ref:Gal 2:15|Galatians 2:15]).
"Wisdom is justified by her deeds" – Jesus defends his fellowship with tax collectors and sinners against the accusations from the Pharisees ([ref:Matt 11:19|Matthew 11:19]).

Paul urges: "Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ has welcomed you." The word "welcome" (προσλαμβάνεσθε) reflects the same principle that Jesus "welcomes" (προσδέχεται) sinners ([ref:Rom 15:7|Romans 15:7]).
